newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Gore to keep SAfrica Syria arms talks confidential.
newsitem.headline: Gore to keep SAfrica Syria arms talks confidential.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore said he will keep discussions with South African leaders about a proposed arms sale with Syria confidential.

In an interview on Saturday, Gore said: "I treat opportunities to discuss such sensitive issues with President Nelson Mandela and Deputy President Thabo Mbeki the same way I treat such conversations with President Clinton -- as matters that must be dealt with confidentially."
He said South Africa was already fully aware of Washington's opposition to the proposed $650 million sale of a laser-guided tank firing control system to Syria.
Gore is expected to raise the matter with Mbeki in private talks on Monday.

Gore is in South Africa at the head of a U.S. delegation which includes five cabinet secretaries for three days of talks to deepen the cooperation between the two countries on trade, economics, science, education, health and the environment. Mbeki heads the South African team to the binational commission.
Gore planned on Sunday to visit the prison on Robben Island, where Mandela was held for 18 years. He then makes courtesy calls on Mandela and retired archbishop Desmond Tutu.

The two countries exchanged angry words last month when the United States warned South Africa against going through with the arms sale to Syria, which Washington classifies as a "state sponsor of terrorism".

Mandela angrily rejected the U.S. criticism as an affront to his country's national pride and independence. Washington warned that providing the system to Syria would result in South Africa losing $120 million of U.S. aid.
But both countries now seem anxious to defuse the issue and Gore welcomed South Africa's stated intention to consider the issue carefully before taking a decision.

Gore said he believed the United States had as strong an interest in seeing South Africa's transition to multi-racial democracy succeed as it had in Russia's building of a free market democratic society.

"In a world beset with racial and ethnic conflicts, from Bosnia to Nagorno-Karabakh to Rwanda, Burundi, Zaire to Cambodia to Cyprus, if South Africa can make this transition, it will be a permanent beacon of hope to humankind," he said.

Gore said the United States had created binational commissions to pursue cooperation across a broad range of issues with only two countries -- South Africa and Russia. He heads the U.S. side to both and has emerged as a leading voice in U.S. foreign policy.

He is also increasingly seen as Clinton's designated heir apparent. Many guests to a reception held in Gore's honour at the U.S. ambassador's residence Saturday said they had come the see and hear the man who could become the next president of the United States.

Gore brushed off internal criticism from white South African leaders of the Mandela government's commitment to democracy. "They have been quite innovative and creative in the South African context of balancing the rights of different ethnic groups, while keeping their eyes on the prize of a non-racial democracy," he said.

For that reason, Gore was determined not to allow the Syrian arms sale to overshadow his trip or sour relations between the two countries. He was aware of South African national sensitivities and intended to raise the issue quietly and carefully.
Gore said that as a native of the South of the United States, he had special appreciation for the way South Africa was putting its past of racial hatred behind it.
"Those of us from the South of the United States...may have an extra added interest in the emotional dimension of this healing process now under way in South Africa," he said.
